utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel. Mark Harmon, Daniel Saxon, April Carter, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, and good afternoon to everyone participating in the proceedings today. Mr. Perisic will be represented by Milos Androvic; Tina Drolec; our case manager, Daniela Tasic; and Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith; and Novak Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Gunj.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will now resume from the point where you -- following the same chronology as was followed in your answers to Mr. Harmon. You said yesterday that you informed your superior Mr. Jovanovic that General Mladic and his entourage were -- of their presence in the Rajac facility only after you were told by Mr. Banduka that you can go and tell him of that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And this was approximately a few days after they arrived?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also said that Mr. Jovanovic seemed surprised when he received the information; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Jovanovic tell you on that occasion how to behave and what to do? Were you issued any instructions by him?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I informed him of the situation and the issue and current situation regarding the food supplies and other resources that they needed, and also what they had at their disposal, and also what their proposal was as to how we could help them on those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And then he issued some instructions to you as your superior?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He instructed me to inform him of anything that I need and that he will relay it to his superiors and that I can start requisitioning these goods.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I assume that in this first period, time-period, which was about a month long, you had occasion to see and talk to Mr. Jovanovic again?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During this period of time, did you ever hear Mr. Jovanovic say that he had ever been contacted from the General Staff by anyone personally?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never heard anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please move into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gunj, can I just ask you one more thing that we did not hear anything about during the evidence in chief. How many of your men, you mentioned this colonel who informed you, Spasojevic or Stevanovic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many men, how many men, your men, were in the facility, I mean, Yugoslav Army men?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time it was only Mr. Spasojevic, and in June there was another soldier under contract, so there were the two of them and myself. We were members of -- the only members from my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I assume that they were there around the clock, 24 hours a day; there would always be someone?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I also understood you to say that you went there occasionally, from time to time. When you say from time to time, what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was there almost non-stop, but very frequently I would have to travel during the day in order to purchase items that we needed and so on, but then I would return in the evening and spend the night there. This would have been maybe every other or every third day, and sometimes I would go away every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please just make a brief pause after my question. Now, tell us, did you hear from your soldiers who were there, or maybe from the locals, that General Mladic went to Gik or to Milanovac? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard this later on from the local people when General Mladic had already moved to another location, and these people told me because they recognised him while he went out for a walk. They recognised and saw him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please now tell the Trial Chamber what Gik is and what --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Ljig. Interpreter's correction: Ljig.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- and what Milanovac is, and how far they are?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not Ljig or Milanovac. These were hamlets not far from the facility, about 5 kilometres at most.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you heard from the villagers, from these hamlets that he took walks in that area in the first -- during this first time-period, the first month?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Mladic left this facility in 1997, and I'm referring to this first visit, you said that -- as far as I understood you, that when you met his security men, the men from his entourage in Topcider, you heard from them that he was also in the Stragari hotel, in that facility, that he went there too?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I told you, I had to go to Topcider -- to that unit from time to time, and there I would meet these men, the security men, and they just mentioned on their own these things from which I drew the conclusion that Mr. Mladic was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was this a fact that was also known to other people in this barracks in Topcider? Generally, did they know that these people were present in the barrack and also about General Mladic's presence?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have any official contact to learn this from them, but I only had occasion to speak to these people outdoors when we were in the yard or on the perimeter, and I would meet these security men, and they would tell me about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And did you notice it later -- did you hear it from someone later on?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't notice any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just try and recap what you said to Mr. Harmon about how many times General Mladic came to your facility together with his entourage. From what you said, your evidence on page 21, yesterday's page 21, you said that the first visit was over a month long, maybe even two months long. This was in the summer of 1997; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Next, you said that he came and stayed up to eight days in late January and early February, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, up to seven days. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In other words, a week. Let's be unspecific and yet clear enough. I understood that in the following years he would come occasionally and stay for a day or so.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he came on several occasions. He would come in the morning and then leave in the afternoon. There were two such visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We are talking now about 1999 and 2000; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1998 and 1999. Approximately, this was at the same time of the year, end of January, early February, and I already mentioned in my earlier evidence that I'm not sure of 2000, whether he came, but if he did it would have been for a shorter period of time and probably at the same season, same time of the year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what you were referring to in 1998, he was there just at one time, the period that you described, end of January, early February?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998, he came in late January, early February, because there was some kind of hunting event there, so he came to our facility in order to seek shelter because there were a lot of people there. And then he came, I can't recall whether this was in autumn or late summer, but he came for one day. And I think, I'm not sure, but I think Mr. Perisic was present too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In other words, in 1998 he came on two occasions, this early visit in late January, early February, and then another visit; when did you say?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say for sure whether this was in early summer or late summer. I know it was warm, but he did come for one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So that was the time when you had an immediate contact with General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. During these subsequent visits, and we are talking about the period after 1998, he never announced his visits, did he?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are talking about the arrivals from [indiscernible]? No, they were announced. I knew I had to prepare the facility for the team that was supposed to arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But nobody called you from the office of the chief of the General Staff to announce those visits?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, nobody did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who called you to announce the visits?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my colleague that I contacted. He was the head of service down there, and before the arrival and the transfer of the team, General Curcin would also -- and General Vukovic also told me to prepare the facility because the activity would take place, and because of the organisational reasons I was in frequent contact with a colleague of mine who was at the head of service down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since you were not in Stragari, you obviously don't know personally whether he was in Stragari all the time between the two visits to Rajac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never there personally, but according to the information that I had from the same people after the first arrival, I realised that he was there all the time, but I was never there personally. I was never on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you understood during the conversation that he was there, but you didn't know whether he was there all the time; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you from my contacts with them and from my subsequent meeting with Mr. Bozovic, the head of Stragari in Belgrade, I knew the gentleman was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bozovic, did he tell you that he was in Stragari all the time?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not say that expressly, but judging from the course of the conversation and the topics that we tackled, it was obvious that he was there. That's what I inferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is what I was going ask you. This was your inference, not the fact that you heard from him; am I right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean my inference, my conclusion?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me put it this way. When they arrived at Rajac for the second time, nobody told you, We were in Stragari all the time before we arrived here?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody told me that expressly; however, from my conversations and contacts with the people who were around -- surrounding that activity, I was convinced that that activity was taking place down there. That's the information that I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just looking for precise information and precise answer to my question. Nobody told you expressly he was there all the time. You concluded that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. Nobody expressly said it, but I concluded that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. And now yesterday, when you were talking about this encounter during the one day arrival at Rajac and when you met with General Perisic, you said that -- this is on page 38 of yesterday's LiveNote, you said that there was General Curcin there. Let me just consult my notes to be very precise in putting my question to you. You said this on page 38, line 21, of yesterday's LiveNote: [In English] "It was one-day stay. General Mladic and General Curcin and General Vukovic with his wife were there, and General Perisic arrived also." [Interpretation] General Perisic arrived later. He did not arrive with them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are right. General Perisic arrived later. They were already there when Perisic arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And yesterday when you described your dialogue with Mr. Perisic, I understood that it was his suggestion, a suggestion on his part, an informal conversation not to speak about these things; it was not an order?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was just a suggestion, informal, on the terrace in front of the hall, and that's how I understood it, just the way I did when I received the first suggestion. This was normal. There were no raised voices. I did not sense that this was an order or anything to the effect of an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So this was a year after the first visit?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if that was in early summer, then it would a bit less than a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just completed my cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Gunj, yesterday my colleague Mr. Lukic showed you Defence Exhibit 55, and he directed your attention to a particular portion of that, which indicated that the order pursuant to which your status had been regulated was issued on the 19th of May, 1997. Do you remember that testimony? If not, I can bring up D55 and show you the document. Do you recall that being the date in which your status as -- actually, let's do it quite easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you bring up D55, please, Registrar, and can you go to page 4. Can we scroll to the bottom of this. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, on the right-hand side, lower right-hand side, Mr. Gunj, there is a set of numbers, and it says "19.5.97." I understood that to be the date on which you received an order. Do you recall that order that you received?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the bottom part of this table where it says that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, sir, the far right-hand side, the far column on the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct. Was that the order that ordered you to become the hotel manager at Rajac and Topcider hotels?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that that was the case. However, as far as I can remember, I assumed my duties towards the end of May or around the 1st of June, rather. And maybe this date indicates the date when the order was actually drafted and issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when was the first time -- actually, prior to this order being drafted, Mr. Gunj, had you ever been to the hotel Topcider and the hotel Rajac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I was in Rajac but not in Topcider.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And prior to the 19th of May, 1997, what were you doing at the hotel Rajac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that was in 1995 or 1996. I was assisting the then-manager with my team of cooks and waiters. The occasion was the celebration of the day of the Army of Yugoslavia for the 1st Army. That was taking place in the facility. He couldn't do it on his own. I had to come to assist him because there was a lot of people, a lot of food. It was a major event that had to be organised, and I was engaged to assist him with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And can you -- what was your prior assignment prior to becoming the manager at the hotel Rajac and Topcider? What were your duties and responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the head of one shift in the central military mess in the Topcider barracks, and I was also the deputy of the head of the hall restaurant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would that position, Mr. Gunj, be reflected in the box, second box from the bottom on the far left?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is reflected above the thing that we have just spoken about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Correct. So it's above the box that says you are the hotel manager at the Topcider and the Rajac facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, you are right. Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you received your orders to become the manager at the hotel Topcider and the hotel Rajac, when was the first time after you received those orders that you went to the hotel Rajac?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean after I received my orders on becoming the manager? I believe that I arrived a few days earlier before assuming my duties, and my colleague and -- who was my predecessor and I were given some time to hand over duties, which means that we were there together for some eight days to hand over the duties and to hand over all the material and equipment that was in the hotels.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. So once you arrived, you had to consult with the predecessor and familiarise yourself with the facilities, familiarise yourself with the materials that were there before you could assume your duty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how long did it take you to become familiar with both the Rajac facility, the hotel, and the Topcider hotel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that it took me some ten days before I assumed my duties. It took me between the 20th of May and the end of June, during which period of time the handover was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much, Mr. Gunj. I have no additional questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall speak French now. What were the administrative procedures and the accountancy procedures which you followed as a manager of these military hotels? You said that you had received no written order for furnishing equipment or food to General Mladic and his entourage, but you were spending money, weren't you, since you were the one who would go and purchase food and whatever was needed; therefore, you were obliged to report from an accountancy point of view. You certainly didn't take this money out of your own salary, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the team arrived at the facility, Mr. Banduka had some funds, some cash on him. He would give me that, and in agreement with him I would go and purchase everything that was necessary to top up the supplies, and gradually supplies started from the military depots. That was the system at the beginning. That food was not accounted for, the food that was bought for cash or the food that was taken from military supplies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, during all the time General Mladic and his entourage were residing in the hotels of this Yugoslav Army, the food and other elements were paid cash during all this period?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in cash. As I've told you in my previous answer, at the beginning a few days into their stay, cash was used to pay for the food, and the cash came from team members, so this was not the money, either mine or from the army. And as we spent all of their supplies, we increased the supplies from the central military supplies. And then as the money increased, we were able to rely more on the supply from the military supplies and less from purchasing goods on the free market.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in such a case you had to justify, when you were taking all these supplies on the allotment of the army, you had to justify the reason why you were asking for all that; isn't it the case?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not the one who had to do that. I suppose this was done by the people who issued me with all these things. I don't know how they did that. I don't know how they defined their duties. As far as I'm concerned, everything that I needed I could take from the supplies. Everything was approved, and I suppose those people had assessed on how to justify for an increased issuance of supply from the depot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PICARD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Gunj, before the very first visit by General Mladic to this facility, what activities on a day-to-day basis took place in this place?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to Rajac hotel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm referring to Rajac hotel. That's where you were, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, we had organisational preparations to tidy up the hotel for its intended purpose, and the purpose was for the hotel to be equipped and tidied up for the rest and recreation of the members of the Army of Yugoslavia and their members of family. We started tidying up and planning how to carry out the necessary works. We started to plan our finances and the timing for all the works that needed to be done in order to prepare hotel to be able to carry out its purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Once you had finished preparations, what then took place on a day-to-day basis in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We started some minimum preparations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are finished with the preparations. Once you were prepared and everything was ready and the hotel was ready to run, what took place? What activities took place in this building?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, the hotel has a purpose. Now, you became a manager there and you say you got there, you prepared it for its purpose. What was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan and the purpose was that in a foreseeable future, since the hotel was in a very poor state of repairs and there was nothing much in the hotel in terms of equipment, we wanted to prepare it to serve for the rest and recreation of the members of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Now, after you had repaired it and you had prepared it, did the members of the army come there on a regular basis? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the army started arriving gradually after General Mladic left, after his first stay with his team. Then the conditions were in place for us to start accommodating members of the army and their families.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question initially was, before Mr. Mladic came there the very first time and after you had prepared this hotel and had repaired it and it was ready for its purpose, what activities on a day-to-day took place in the hotel? Did anything take place or not?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are getting no translation.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no activities taking place. Nobody arrived at the hotel, neither the members of the army or their family members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And during Mr. Mladic's stay in the hotel, did these people come? Did anybody come to the hotel outside his entourage?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody, just Mr. Mladic and his entourage. There were no other guests. There were no other activities taking place. Mr. Mladic and his team were there on their own, as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What staff complement did you have when you first -- when you finished preparing the hotel for its purpose? Even before Mr. Mladic came to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I assumed my duties, there were just two professionals in the hotel. A few days later, one of them resigned and left the hotel and just one remained. So for the first month before Mr. Mladic arrived, there were just some of my subordinate units from Belgrade who were commissioned to do the works, and those were different handymen, decorators, who were brought in to gradually and slowly prepare the hotel for its purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we try to stay a little chronological and clear. I'm now talking to you about the time when the preparations had been finished. Okay. You've told us that you were -- two of your professionals were there. Now, amongst the three of you and between the two of you after the other one had resigned, you attended to the cleaning and the cooking and everything that had to be done in the hotel? Just the two of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We attended to what we were actually able to do, and the command helped by sending teams of electricians, plumbers, and house painters, because the building was rather derelict. It was in a poor condition, so it needed quite a lot of men to work on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Gunj, can we please understand each other. I'm done with the preparation of the building. I'm now in the running of the building. Can you please forget about going back to the preparation of the building. Just listen to the questions that I'm putting to you, and try to answer the questions as I put you to them. Don't formulate the question for yourself and answer it. I'm asking you, when this building was ready to run and the preparations were finished, did you and your two colleagues before the one resigned and you and your one colleague after the other had resigned, just the three of you, deal with the day-to-day work that had to be done in this building, in the running of the business, not in the preparation?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as we were able to, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And do I understand you to say that when guests came to the hotel, you catered for them, just the two of you, you did the cooking, the cleaning of the rooms, everything that needs to be done between the two of you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there weren't any guests. They only started arriving after Mr. Mladic and his entourage left the hotel for the first time. It was only then that the hotel gradually started receiving guests. Before that, the only thing we did was preparing the hotel, and then Mladic's arrival interrupted those preparations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But I'm talking to you about the time when you were running the hotel, sir. You keep going back to preparations. Obviously, when I'm talking about the time when you were running the hotel, I'm referring also to the time after Mladic left. When the guests came to the hotel after Mladic left, what complement of staff did you have to cater for your guests?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was when we started receiving new staff members. We received two or three new staff members then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And when General Mladic was there for the month, were you there with the two professionals or with the one only? In other words, was it during the time when you had the two of them, or was it after one had resigned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Mladic arrived with his entourage, there was just me and another staff member. Ten days later, we received another professional soldier so that at the time of Mr. Mladic's stay there, there were two professional staff members in addition to myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And were any instructions given to these two about Mr. Mladic's stay at the hotel, to keep it secret like you were told? Are you aware of any instructions being given to them?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they did not receive any instructions from anyone else, but I conveyed to them what had been said to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You just told them what was told to you, or did you ask them also to do the same?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told them what I had been told, and I said that they should do the same, that they should abide by that just as I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. It's time for a break. We'll come back at quarter to 4.00. I beg your pardon. I'm sorry. Okay. We still have more time. Let me move to the next topic, then. You indicated during cross-examination this afternoon that Mr. Mladic, who would go out for a walk to some hamlet in the neighbourhood, apart from going for these walks, are you aware of him having gone in and out with his entourage or even alone for other destinations during his stay there? Was he moving in and out of the hotel freely, or was he just staying in the hotel except for these little walks?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the first few days, Mr. Mladic stayed in the hotel all the time. After some ten days or so, he, with a few members of his entourage, began going out in civilian clothes on his own initiative and to take walks along the footpaths, and his walks grew longer and longer, and then they would come back. I observed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are saying in civilian clothes. Were they in military clothes or in some uniform of sorts while they were in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, they wore civilian clothes all the time. They were wearing civilian clothes when they arrived, and they wore civilian clothes throughout their stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When they went out apart from the walks, did they drive out in their cars, or what happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not go out in vehicles or cars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did they receive any visitors other than members of the army that you have already told us about who you said visited them? Did they receive any other visitors apart from those people?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, they received no other visitors apart from the persons I've already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Am I right to say that you indicated in your evidence in chief that Mr. Mladic had brought his own cook?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That cook, did he cook for him for the entire stay, or did you ever have to help with your staff?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That cook cooked food for him and his whole entourage. One of my men occasionally assisted with the washing up or clearing away of garbage, but he did not participate in preparing the food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any questions arising from the Bench's questions, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, I have just a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Gunj, you said that General Mladic and members of his entourage went on some walks on the footpaths. Is the hotel Rajac in a rural area? Is it an urban area? Is it an isolated area? How would you describe it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN GUNJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Rajac hotel is on a mountain, a small mountain far away from other inhabited places, and around our villages and hamlets and mostly weekend cottages belonging to people who spend weekends and holidays there. So the nearest villages are about a kilometre and a half away.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Gunj, thank you so much. This brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you for coming to testify at the Tribunal. You are now excused, and you may stand down. Please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see you going on your feet, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Saxon assumes this position, could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, I believe you are calling the witness. Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Sir, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Mladen Mihajlovic. I'm a retired general from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You say you are a retired general?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you serve both in the JNA and later what was called the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, General, approximately for how many years did you serve as a military officer?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Forty years. Forty years of -- actual years of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at the time of your retirement, what was your specific rank?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel-general. I was retired as a colonel-general.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What year did you retire from the army?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I retired in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you have a particular specialty within the army?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My specialty is engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In March of 1991, what was your position?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I became the chief of the operations section and also the deputy chief of the engineering administration with the Main Staff -- the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say you became chief of the operations section, did you mean to use the word "section" or the word "sector"?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Administration for engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I understand it's administration for engineering. You mentioned that you were the chief of the -- never mind, I will move on. Briefly, what was the work of the engineering administration?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: The engineering administration at whose head I was at the time had to monitor the situation with combat readiness, especially the engineering units, to propose certain measures and take steps in order to ensure that the combat readiness is improved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, when we refer to the engineering administration, what kind of work are we talking about? What kind of activities are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was involved in drawing up plans for combat training in engineering at the army level, and also providing equipment for engineering -- for the engineering arm with engineering equipment and also units of other arms of the army, providing them with engineering equipment. It also drafted proposals for the development of new technical equipment and their introduction as part of the standard equipment of the army. It also drew up or prepared texts for rules of combat use -- for use of engineering units in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Did the engineering administration deal with materials such as mines and explosives?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. In 1993, did you take up another position?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Toward the end of 1993, I was appointed chief of the engineering administration with the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So you were then a member of the General Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And for how many years were you a member of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Until my retirement in 1999. In other words, for six years I was the chief of the engineering administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And during those six years, did you become familiar with the structure and the work of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in general terms. I'm not acquainted with every detail, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Let's talk for a few moments about the structure of the General Staff of the VJ. In October 1993, when you became chief of the engineering department, who was the chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I think that at this time the chief of the General Staff was Mr. -- General Perisic. I'm not sure exactly whether it was a bit before that time or a little later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did the chief of the General Staff have an office to assist him with his work?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was that sometimes called a cabinet?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Cabinet, yes, that's how I know it. The cabinet of the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the Chief of the General Staff have a deputy?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In addition to the members of the cabinet and the deputy of the chief, did the General Staff have other members?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: At the second level, there were assistant chiefs of the General Staff who were at the same time the chiefs of sectors for certain areas and operations in the various branches of the army, as well as chiefs of independent administrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just very briefly, can you name some of the sectors which had assistants to the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already mentioned the operations sector, the sectors for the various branches for the land forces, the air forces, and the navy. These were all various sectors. Then there was the logistics sector, and I believe the informations and signals sector or communications sector. There were also some independent administrations for morale, for intelligence, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did these assistants to the Chief of the General Staff have a command function over VJ units?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Then what function did these assistants have?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've already mentioned for the engineering administration, the same kind of work was within the purview of these various sectors within their own areas of work. I don't know if there was a sector that also had a unit attached to it or under its command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did these assistants for different sectors provide advice to the Chief of the General Staff about their sectors?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There is no function of counsellor in the army, but the chiefs of sector, at the same time they provided advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned the land army sector of the VJ. What was the land army sector comprised of?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: The ground forces sector had a department, an operations department, and it also had administrations of various arms of the army, such as infantry artillery, armoured forces, biological warfare, chemical, and nuclear warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the land army sector also contained the engineering administration; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And as the head of the engineering section -- administration, who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I was subordinate to the chief of the sector for the ground forces, or land army, directly subordinate to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned an operations sector of the VJ. What was the function of this sector?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: As a rule, I can say that this sector dealt with planning. I don't know what all the competences of all the other sectors were, but mainly they dealt with planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the assistant to the Chief of the General Staff for the operation sector have an important role?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: That was the first sector that brought together the proposals coming from the other sectors, the information coming from the army, and prepared the basic combat documents for the needs of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. You mentioned there was a logistics sector of the VJ, logistics sector of the VJ General Staff. What was the function of the logistics sector?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: The main function was supplying the army with equipment and materiel of all kinds.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know if the logistics sector had different departments or units?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: The logistics sector to the best of my recollection had an operations administration for the rear, a planning organ, and it had the administrations office services, the quartermaster service, the technical service, the traffic service, the medical service. I think I've enumerated them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Let's talk a little bit more about your role as the chief of the engineering administration. What were your responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: As I've mentioned, primarily my main responsibility was to monitor the development of the units of the arm of service and other units as regards their ability to use engineering equipment and supplying them with engineering equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Were you ever involved in decisions regarding the replenishment of engineering equipment or materiel to parts of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the engineering administration, we kept records and monitored the situation as regards replenishment; and depending on the resources available, we made plans for replenishing the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And in addition to plans, did you ever make recommendations about replenishment or purchase of materials?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. The replenishment implies requisition, procurement. If the equipment is new, there has to be a procedure for introducing new types of equipment. All this was done by the administration in order to replenish the units according to their establishment and their needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you made recommendations pertaining to replenishment of materiel, to whom would you send your recommendations?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: The replenishment system went according to plan. Periodic plans were drawn up, 5-year plans, 1-year plans, where every arm and every service based on the situation in their units drew up a plan for every year by type of equipment. These plans were actually a wish list. They weren't usually implemented because the resources available were meager, so the wish list had to be reduced to whatever was possible. There were sanctions imposed in those years. There was no import. Our own industry was having difficulties, so replenishment was a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, General, but my question was a bit different. My question was simply this: When you made --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Oh, it's my fault because I think my question was not clear. When you made recommendations about what equipment to replenish -- should be replenished, what equipment should not be replenished, to whom would you make these recommendations? To whom would you send these recommendations?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: The recommendations were sent according to a prescribed procedure. They went to the sector for the ground forces. They would send this on to the logistics sector. Then it would go to the ministry or to the Chief of the General Staff. I'm not quite sure about that part. And then, as I've already mentioned, the financial organs of the Ministry of Defence sent the plans back, telling us what funds we had available, what the quotas were, what we had to work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to stop you there. You mentioned that your recommendation would go to the ministry or to the Chief of the General Staff. Would the Chief of the General Staff, to your knowledge, then make decisions about what materiels would be replenished and what would not?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: He didn't make decisions about individual materiels or pieces of equipment. The overall plan was approved by him and then sent on to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. To your knowledge, did the Chief of the General Staff of the VJ have a collegium?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a collegium, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what was the purpose of this collegium? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was an advisory body which met from time to time to consider certain topical issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Did the collegium have permanent members?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I think the permanent members were the assistants -- his assistants or, rather, the chiefs of the sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And was the Chief of the General Staff a permanent member of the collegium?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's logical in my view. He presided over the collegium.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Between 1993 and 1995, were you ever invited to attend the collegium of the Chief of the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The lower-level chiefs, the chiefs at the third level were invited occasionally when there was a discussion on the agenda that had to do with their field of activity or their competencies. In my case, it would be engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can you recall, approximately how often would you be -- were you invited to attend the collegium during those years?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: After all this time, I'm not sure how many times I was invited, but I think there was a period - I don't know whether it was the first or the last period - when a plan was changed and we -- chiefs of arms of service attended once a month. Whether this was in 1994 or 1995, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you attended those collegiums, was General Perisic present?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he or his deputy if he was absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What kinds of issues were discussed when you were present at the collegium meetings?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, the usual issues: Briefing by his subordinates on the tasks carried out in the army; the military and political situation prevailing in the area; work plans; and specific problems that had arisen between two collegium meetings. That was more or less what the meetings were about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did General Perisic run these meetings?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe how General Perisic ran the meetings? What would the dynamic be like?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, the dynamic was military. There was a plan, to the best of my recollection. There was a certain order in which the individual participants would take the floor. They were given a brief period of time, I'm not sure exactly how long, but they had a certain time in which to brief him. He would put questions for clarification, and that's how it went.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: During those meetings, did General Perisic indicate that he understood the issues being discussed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He would ask for clarification occasionally. If everything was clear -- well, he behaved normally in compliance with military norms and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: How would you describe General Perisic as an officer?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was a soldier. When you say soldier, that implies his appearance, his bearing, his manner of issuing orders. I don't know what else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you refer to General Perisic's manner of issuing orders, can you be a bit more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you are referring to. He would look at the agenda and tell people to take the floor. He would put questions if he didn't understand something or give his approval or non-approval. He would say, Work on this a bit more, Elaborate this further, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to move on to another topic. General, are you familiar with the term "war reserves" as it was used in the JNA and the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: War reserves are reserves of all the materiel needed by the army to wage war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And is there only -- well, how many kinds of war reserves are there or were there at that time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: There were several levels with soldiers by units and in the central depots.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And did the war reserves in the central depot, central depots, did those reserves have a particular name, or did you refer -- were those reserves referred to by a particular description?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer that question. I don't know what you mean. There was, for example, the quartermaster depot, the lethal weapons depot. I didn't know the locations of all these depots.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Above the unit level of reserves, was there another kind of war reserve?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, those were the overall reserves outside the units which were kept in the depots of the rear bases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. And you mentioned reserves that were kept in the central depots. Can you be a little bit more specific? Who controlled these central depots?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't deal with that, but I think this was -- this fell under the rear organ, from the sector in the General Staff to the corps command, and it ended with the bases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did the General Staff of the army maintain war reserves?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I can't answer that. I don't know whether they were called the General Staff's reserves. There was a logistics base, a central logistics base, I think it was called the 68th [as interpreted], and it was under the jurisdiction of the real logistics sector, but whether they had their own basis, I really couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: When you say it was -- first of all, you referred to a base, and the English translation says "68th." Did you say 68th or 608th?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not sure whether the witness said 68th or 608th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just once more for the record, General, if you could speak up a little bit. Did you say 68 or 608?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. When you say the 608th logistics base was under the jurisdiction of the logistics sector, that's a sector of the General Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to move to the topic of requests for assistance to the Army of Yugoslavia. General, to your knowledge, between 1993 and 1995, did the Army of Republika Srpska, the VRS, ever make requests to the VJ, the Army of Yugoslavia for equipment and materiels?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Was there a procedure established for the processing of such requests?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And were you familiar with this procedure?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And how did you become familiar with this procedure?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: My superior told me what the procedure was. He was the chief of the sector for the land army or the ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do you know where your superior received information about what the procedure would be?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I can say that this is what probably happened, but I can't know what my superior -- what all the things he did. But anyway, that's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think my question wasn't clear. Do you know who explained this procedure or gave this procedure to your superior, the assistant for land army sector?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I assume this was done at the level of the General Staff. Whether it was through the cabinet or at the collegium or by the chief, that I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What was the first step in this procedure in terms of making a request from the VRS or the SVK to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how requests came to the General Staff, but I do know how they reached me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Maybe let me start a little bit earlier. If the VRS wanted to request assistance from the VJ, what part, what unit of the VRS was supposed to send a request to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: From the documents I was able to see, the General Staff or the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska - I've forgotten now what its precise name was - sent a request to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If the request from the VRS Main Staff only concerned engineering materiel and equipment, what would the VJ General Staff do with the request, according to the procedure?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: For a time, I would receive a copy of the original request from the cabinet, and there would be a handwritten note on it saying, Consider this request, Supply this if possible, or the chief of the cabinet would write a note on a scrap of paper, For consideration, The chief says this should be considered, If possible the material should be provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And do you recall who the person or persons were who would make these handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: The Chief of the General Staff in the upper right-hand corner wrote by hand, Look into this, consider it, and he would initial that. And the cover letter, which was actually an informal scrap of paper, would provide instructions as to what the administration should do. And we would then take the document into consideration and respond to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before we go to your response, at some point did this procedure that you've just described, receiving the request from the VJ General Staff, from the cabinet, did that change a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: The relations between the two staffs, I think, did not change. What changed was the procedure we used. I may be wrong when I say what came first and what came second, but this procedure did not go directly from the cabinet to me, but it went to the logistics sector, and then the ground army, and then the engineers, and then the route back would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So at some point, these requests were sent via the logistics sector before they got to your administration; is that it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what then would you do after you received a request, request for engineering materiel or equipment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that request, with his associates and especially the desk officer in charge of that, my deputy, we considered the situation and then we provided our position as to what needed to be done. Usually if there was a request for one quantity, we would reduce that because that's what we could provide; a level of replenishment was not satisfactory in any way. Then we would send the reply back, i.e., to the sector for the land army, and from there it went to the logistics sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: From the logistics sector, where would your reply go?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I can't say. I suppose that this is where everything ended. All the suggestions and proposals ended up there, and a document would be drafted there for the Chief of the General Staff's consideration and final decision-making.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Suppose the Chief of the General Staff approved one of these requests; who would carry out the transfer of equipment or materiel to the VRS or the SVK?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: This does not fall within my purview. I never dealt with that, but I suppose it would be the logistics organs, the executive organs of the 608th base, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me change the scenario just a little bit, General. Suppose the original request from the VRS Main Staff or the SVK Main Staff asked for different kind of equipment and not just engineering equipment. How would that request be processed?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: In the sector for land army, that's where the desk officers from all the administrations would go to. All the desk officers that had to do with the particular request, they would photocopy the request, they would bring them over to the respective administrations, and we would follow the procedure. We would -- took the request under advisement. I would draft a reply initially, and then I would send it to the sector of the land army. They would compile all of our inputs, and then they would send to the centre for logistics as I've already explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just a few moments ago, before we move on, you mentioned that you would reduce often the quantity that was requested because you said the level of replenishment was not satisfactory in any way. Why wasn't the level of replenishment satisfactory during those years, 1993 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: It was not satisfactory even before, and during that period, the materiel was being used and there were no resources to replenish the quantities that were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you a few documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, may we please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, this procedure that you've described for us, how requests were made, sent to the General Staff, requests were forwarded to you, et cetera, was this procedure always followed to the letter?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I followed it. I saw documents. You showed me documents from which I could see that some others did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, can we move into private session now, please. My apologies again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session. 16 [Private session] [Confidentiality partially lifted by order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can -- if I can ask the Registry's assistance, I'd like to show one of the documents that I mentioned to the Chamber earlier that the OTP recently received from Serbia. It would be now part of 65 ter 7899 with document ID 0646-6630.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to know why we are in private session? Why is this document shown in private session? I really don't understand the reason behind this decision. Could Mr. Saxon maybe explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Because the government of Serbia asked that the Prosecution use this document in private session until they had a chance to make further submissions on whether this document could be public or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was it the condition of disclosing the document to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am happy with the explanation. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you could direct your attention to the document that is on the screen in front of you, General, you'll see this is a document -- it's dated the 11th of March, 1994, from the engineering administration, and is that your signature on the bottom of the document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the document is titled in English: "Accordance For Redistribution of Engineering Assets, Arms, and Military Equipment For VRS." And this document is being sent, apparently, to Military Post 9808 in Belgrade. Do you recall, what was Military Post 9808?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that this is the military post of the 608th logistics base.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And further down, it says: "Based upon a request by the Main Staff of Republika Srpska, your administration approves the redistribution of engineering military equipment and arms." What was the equipment that you were approving being provided to the VRS in this document?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: This is a rocket device to make -- to open passages through minefields that we had in the army. At the time, they were already obsolete. They were no longer used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why give them to the VRS if they are obsolete?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They wanted them. They were in a good state of repair. They worked properly, but they were not used by the troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The VJ troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] VJ troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see up top, there is a number underneath the heading on the upper left-hand side, confidential number 44-2. And if we can scroll down a little bit in both versions, there is a handwritten note saying that three pieces of the UROP have been issued to the VRS on 14th of May, 1995. Do you know wrote that note?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not write that, neither did my administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. General, when you drafted this document and you signed it, were you following the procedure that you described to us a few moments ago?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously that was not the case. However, there is no preceding document based on which I drafted the request the way I did. It is only to be assumed, but I don't want to speculate. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you say, Obviously that is not the case, is that because this document -- well, tell us why. Why do you say obviously it was not the case that you were following the procedure that you described to us before?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: I did not violate any rules intentionally or consciously. I suppose that there was something in the request that prompted me to act the way I did. Since there's only one piece of equipment in question and that piece of equipment was under my jurisdiction and authority, I believe that this was done in order to shorten the route, shorten the procedure in a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay. What is it about this document that shortened the route of the normal procedure?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't return the document to the Chief of the General Staff or the logistics sector but directly to the base as the executive organ because this document dealt with just one device, a device from my jurisdiction. I believe that one would find that in the preliminary document, that the preliminary document would explain the subsequent procedure. However, that document does not exist, and I can't prove anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that this document be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You want it marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, and my case manager is providing me with some important information. As 65 ter 0789.06.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought this was 65 ter 7899, ID number 0646-6630.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, and in order to work with these additional documents that we've recently received, we've given these new documents a sub-number, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But now -- and the reason why you want it marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. It was pursuant to the agreement that I had with the Defence and to the leave that I was granted earlier today by Your Honours because it is not formally part of our 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. I had completely forgotten. Okay. This document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number and marked for identification under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P621 marked for identification under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honour. If we could turn, now, please, if we could call up on our screen also part of 65 ter 7899 but with the document ID 0646-6629. And this would be 789.05.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, this is another document. Do you see your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: This document is dated the 16th of May, 1995, and up at the top left-hand corner it has confidential number 260-1. These confidential numbers, were they -- were they used to keep a record of the documents issued by your administration to identify them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: That's the way documents were graded. One of the grades was confidential, strictly confidential, state secret, so this is a qualification, the way documents were graded or qualified.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And the number here, for example, 260-1?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: This is an administrative number for the registration purposes from a book into which the documents were filed and recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. Again, this document is addressed to Military Post 9808 in Belgrade, and again we see in the first paragraph that the engineering administration is approving the transfer of engineering equipment, and below that we see three pieces of UROP. So is this the same equipment that was discussed in the previous document? Same kind of equipment, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: The same kind and the same procedure. However, three more pieces were requested as far as I can see, and in the bottom part of the document, you can see the explanation showing that the total number requested was six, and we're talking about the same device.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we also see here in that last paragraph a reference to confidential number 44-2, dated 11 of March, 1994. So is this document referring back to the document that we looked at previously?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, I would ask that this document be marked for identification under seal, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number, marked for identification, and kept under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P622 marked for identification under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One moment, please, Your Honour. If we could please see on our screens now 65 ter 7899.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, this is a document, it's numbered 260-2 dated the 15th of May, 1995, and the subject refers to consent on engineers' weapons and military equipment handover for the VRS. Again, we see it's directed to Military Post 9808 in Belgrade, and if you look at the first paragraph, it says: "Pursuant to the Army of Republika Srpska Main Staff demand ..." there's number and a date, "... and the Yugoslav Army chief of General Staff consent, engineers administration as a tactical holder has approved the handover of the following engineers' weapons and military equipment without allowance."

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is my document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see a listing of mines and anti-personnel devices below, plastic explosive. And then we see reference to the six UROP devices that had been approved previously. My question is --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Here, you are sending this document pursuant to the request of the VRS and pursuant to the consent of the Chief of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army. Is this document then consistent with the procedure that you've described to us previously about how these kinds of requests should be handled?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN MIHAJLOVIC
